6: is a stack-based programming language.

9: Your evaluator has to support the following words:
10: 
11: - `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` (integer arithmetic)
12: - `DUP`, `DROP`, `SWAP`, `OVER` (stack manipulation)
13: 
14: Your evaluator also has to support defining new words using the customary syntax: `: word-name definition ;`.
15: 
16: To keep things simple the only data type you need to support is signed integers of at least 16 bits size.
17: 
18: You should use the following rules for the syntax: a number is a sequence of one or more (ASCII) digits, a word is a sequence of one or more letters, digits, symbols or punctuation that is not a number.
19: (Forth probably uses slightly different rules, but this is close enough.)
20: 
21: Words are case-insensitive.

## Summary

Implemented the Forth evaluator in `forth.go` (the only file changed):

- **`Forth`** — iterates over input lines, tokenizing with `strings.Fields`. It handles `: name body... ;` definitions and otherwise executes tokens, returning the final stack (an empty but non-nil slice when the stack ends empty, as the `1 drop` case requires).
- **Definition handling** — names are lowercased; defining a number (`: 1 2 ;`, `: -1 2 ;`) is rejected. The body is compiled at definition time: references to user-defined words are expanded to their current bodies, matching real Forth compilation semantics. This is what makes the two tricky cases work:
  - *"can use different words with the same name"*: `bar` keeps the old `foo` (5) even after `foo` is redefined to 6.
  - *"can define word that uses word with the same name"*: the second `: foo foo 1 + ;` resolves the inner `foo` to the previous definition (`10`), yielding 11.
- **Execution** — tokens are classified as numbers (`strconv.Atoi`, so `-1` works), user-defined words (checked first so they can override built-ins like `: swap dup ;`), or built-ins. All word lookup is case-insensitive.
- **Built-ins** — `+ - * / dup drop swap over` with proper stack-arity errors ("empty stack" / "only one value on the stack") and a divide-by-zero error; division is integer division (`8 3 /` → 2).
